questions.q: A quality manager asks if your complaint classifier works on their complaints, not your examples. Where should most of your eval cases come from?
options: Cases you write at your desk to cover each category cleanly
Examples generated by an LLM so you get many cases quickly
Their historical complaints and exception logs, labeled with what a person decided
The demo cases you already know the solution handles well
questions.why: Real history and exception logs carry the messy input and edge cases that break systems in production.

questions.q: While labeling cases, two subject matter experts give different answers for the same invoice. What is the best response?
options: Treat it as a finding: the rule is ambiguous and the client must decide it before the AI can follow it
Use the label from the more senior expert and move on
Drop the case from the set so it does not lower the score
Label it yourself based on what seems most logical
questions.why: Expert disagreement shows the process itself is unclear, so the client needs to set a rule first.

questions.q: Your 40-case eval set scores 95 percent, but almost every case is a normal invoice. What is the main problem?
options: The set is too small; any set under 100 cases is invalid
The score is too high, which proves the labels are wrong
Normal invoices should be removed so only hard cases remain
Coverage: without edge cases like duplicates or missing PO numbers the high score means very little
questions.why: A set with many easy cases and no edge cases gives a high score that does not reflect real risk.

questions.q: You are tuning prompts every day against your eval set. Why keep a small held-back group you do not look at while tuning?
options: So you can add those cases later if the score drops
So you have an honest final check that the prompt was not fitted to the cases you tuned on
Because the held-back cases are the ones the SME has not labeled yet
To save API cost by running fewer cases each day
questions.why: Tuning on every case makes the score flatter you; untouched cases give an honest final check.

questions.q: The sponsor wants one number: how accurate is the invoice assistant? You have 90 percent overall. What should you report alongside it?
options: Nothing more; sponsors only want one number
The pass rate by case type, the number of cases behind it, the dangerous errors and the main failure causes
The model name and token count for each case
A promise that the next prompt version will reach 100 percent
questions.why: One overall number can hide poor results on the edge cases that matter most.

questions.q: In your eval run, one invoice that should be needs_review was marked approve, and one clean invoice was sent to review. Which failure matters more?
options: The clean invoice sent to review, because it wastes a clerk's time
Both are equal, since each counts as one failure in the pass rate
Neither, because the overall pass rate is still above target
The needs_review case marked approve, because it skipped a person and could cost money
questions.why: Errors have different costs; letting a risky case pass without review is the dangerous kind.

questions.q: Your pass rate dropped and a colleague wants to try three new prompt ideas right away. What should you do first?
options: Read every failed case, note what went wrong, group the notes by cause and fix the biggest cause
Try all three prompt ideas at once and keep whichever scores best
Switch to a larger model, since failures are usually the model's fault
Remove the failing cases from the set and rerun
questions.why: Error analysis tells you why it fails, and some causes are bad data or wrong labels, not the prompt.

questions.q: You want to use an LLM-as-judge to grade reply drafts. What makes it trustworthy enough to rely on?
options: Use the largest model available as the judge
Ask the judge one broad question such as 'is this reply good?'
Have the SME grade 20 or 30 outputs by hand, run the judge on the same ones and check how often they agree
Run the judge once and accept its grades if they look reasonable
questions.why: A judge is a measuring tool that must be checked against human grades before you trust it.

questions.q: An AI step drafts internal meeting summaries that users read and edit anyway. Another step sends payment approvals. How should you place review gates?
options: Review both, since every AI output needs a person
Review neither, since reviewers slow everything down
Sample-review the payments weekly and always review the summaries
Always review the payment step; the meeting summaries can have no review gate
questions.why: Gates go where harm is high or irreversible; actions that move money always need a person.

questions.q: A compliance lead says auditors will not accept 'the AI decided'. Which audit record lets you reconstruct a decision months later?
options: The final decision and the date it was made
Case id, input, AI output as shown, model and prompt version, reviewer, decision, reason and timestamps
The AI output and the model name only
A weekly summary of how many cases were approved
questions.why: Auditors need to follow one case end to end, including what the system knew and who decided.

questions.q: After go-live, reviewers approve 99 percent of AI suggestions within a few seconds each. What is the most likely risk?
options: The AI is now perfect and the gate can be removed
The audit table is missing a CHECK constraint
The gate has become theatre; people are clicking approve without really checking
The eval set has too many edge cases
questions.why: If review is slow or confusing or always the same, people rubber-stamp and the gate stops working.

questions.q: A teammate wants to call the LLM directly from front-end JavaScript on a static page to save time. What is the problem?
options: Everything in a static page is visible to anyone, so the API key would be exposed
Static pages cannot make network requests
Static hosting is too expensive for a demo
Static pages do not work with HTML and CSS
questions.why: Secrets must stay on a server or function, never in code that ships to the browser.

questions.q: The client's IT team says everything must run inside their own cloud account, and the service needs a background worker. Which option fits best?
options: A container, because it suits long-running processes and many enterprise IT teams already review and run them
A static page hosted on GitHub Pages
A serverless function, because it has no time or memory limits
Running it from your laptop with a shared link
questions.why: Containers suit long-running jobs and client-owned platforms, and IT teams often know how to operate them.

questions.q: Before choosing where to deploy a POC, what should you start from?
options: The platform you know best, so you build fastest
The cheapest option on a pricing page
The client: where their other apps run, what their security team approves and who will maintain it
Whatever the newest serverless product offers
questions.why: Pick the simplest option the client's IT can approve and support after you leave.

questions.q: A developer notices an API key was committed to Git last week and deletes that commit. Is that enough?
options: Yes, deleting the commit removes the key everywhere
No; assume it is leaked, revoke the key and issue a new one
Yes, as long as the repository is private
No; you also need to rename the environment variable
questions.why: History and copies can still hold the key, so the only safe move is to revoke and replace it.

questions.q: Someone tweaks a prompt and the change quietly lowers quality in production. What would have caught it?
options: A linter that checks the YAML workflow file
Deploying the change straight to prod and watching for complaints
Keeping prompts outside Git so they can be changed faster
An eval gate in CI that runs the eval set and fails the pull request below an agreed pass rate
questions.why: An eval gate marks the pull request red so a prompt change that breaks quality cannot be merged by accident.

questions.q: The client wants to check a release before it goes live. Where should they do that, and with what build?
options: In dev, where builders can change things while they test
In prod, behind a feature flag, with a separate build
In the test environment, using the same build that will then be promoted to prod
On your laptop during a screen share
questions.why: Test mirrors production, and promoting the tested build avoids surprises from a different artifact.

questions.q: A user says the assistant gave a wrong answer yesterday, but your logs only record errors. Why is that a problem?
options: Error logs are too large to search
Logs cannot hold the prompt version
Wrong answers always raise an error, so the log is enough
The wrong answer was a successful request, so nothing was logged to explain it
questions.why: You need records of successful requests, with inputs, outputs and versions, to explain a bad answer.

questions.q: The app has no errors and full uptime, yet the reviewer edit rate has risen each week for a month. What is most likely happening?
options: Quality is drifting, for example from new input layouts or a model update
Nothing; no errors means the system is healthy
The alert limits are set too low
Reviewers are getting faster at their work
questions.why: An LLM app can be up and quietly wrong; edit rate and eval reruns reveal drift.

questions.q: A request uses many input tokens and fewer output tokens. How do you work out its cost?
options: Total tokens times the input price
Input tokens times the input price plus output tokens times the output price, using current provider prices
Output tokens times the output price only, since input is free
A fixed price per request taken from last year's invoice
questions.why: Providers price input and output tokens separately, and prices change, so read current rates.
